There is a well-known theory about probability called Bayes’ Theorem. The Theorem is a mathematical formula used to determine the probability of an event based on prior knowledge related to that event. A description can be found below.   
   
![][image1]  
*P(A|B) is a conditional probability. It estimates the probability of event A occurring given that B is true.* 

*P(B|A) is also a conditional probability, estimating the probability of event B occurring given that A is true* 

*P(A) and P(B) are the probabilities that A and B will happen, respectively, without any specified conditions.* 

 

**Now that you understand Bayes’ Theorem, calculate the likelihood that a given test subject has a rare disease when the test comes back positive. P(A) is the probability that the subject has the disease. P(B) is the false/positive test.** 

Set P(A) \= .03, given that there is a 3% chance of having the rare disease

Set P(B|A)= .99, given that the test is 99% accurate if the subject has the rare disease

Set P(B |not A) (Probability B given not A)= .02 to accommodate the potential false positives at a 2% rate.

Now calculate and print… 

1\.        P(not A)  
2\.        P(B) (hint: [The Law of Total Probability](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_of_total_probability) will be necessary in calculating this)  
3\.        P(A|B)

using a Python script. P(A|B) will give you the probability that the subject has the rare disease given that the test is positive.

After running the Python script, analyze the results you got in terms of why P(A|B) might be lower than the test’s 99% accuracy. What implications does 99% test accuracy assume? What was the biggest struggle in coding these calculations?
